Vigil: Runtime Enforcement of Behavioral Specifications in AI Agent Skills

Ying Li1, Yanju Chen2, Hongbo Wen3, Bosi Zhang4, Hanzhi Liu3, Peiran Wang1, Yu Feng3, Yuan Tian1 Affiliation: 1University of California, Los Angeles  2University of California, San Diego
3University of California, Santa Barbara  4Riema Labs
Abstract

Agentic systems increasingly act through third-party skills, allowing model-generated decisions to affect files, communication channels, and cyber-physical devices. These skills often include natural-language specifications that define access permissions, disclosure limits, execution privileges, and required preconditions. Although such specifications describe the intended boundaries of skill behavior, they do not by themselves provide executable runtime enforcement. Enforcing them raises a contextual granularity challenge: even when a policy is written for a particular task context, a monitor must still decide which events to observe, what state to retain, how far across the execution to reason, and where to intervene. Choosing the wrong granularity can either block benign executions or miss violations that emerge only across multiple actions. Most existing enforcement mechanisms, however, assume a fixed event model or enforcement point.

In this work, we present Vigil, an end-to-end runtime enforcement framework for agentic systems. Vigil checks an agent’s actual execution trace against behavioral policies from skill specifications, operator-defined constraints, and global rules spanning multiple skills. To make such policies executable, Vigil introduces a policy language that captures context-specific enforcement requirements over agent-tool events, including temporal dependencies, argument constraints, and value-flow conditions. The language is paired with symbolic evaluation rules that translate policies into SMT constraints over finite traces, allowing Vigil to detect violations that depend on event order, argument relationships, or cross-call value flow rather than relying on fixed single-call filters. When a violation is detected, Vigil localizes the responsible invocation and its relevant trace context. On real LLM-agent runs spanning office-document, operational, and engineering tasks, Vigil detects policy violations with over 95% recall and a false-positive rate below 10%. Vigil also uncovers real-world skill-specification defects in deployed skill ecosystems, which we reported through responsible disclosure and received acknowledgments from affected vendors, including NVIDIA.

I Introduction

Large-language-model (LLM) agents are rapidly transitioning from conversational assistants to autonomous operators that read private documents, modify repositories, and orchestrate physical workflows. The capabilities behind this reach are increasingly packaged as skills: reusable bundles of instructions, scripts, and tool interfaces that major vendors now ship across assistant [1], developer [2], cloud [3, 4], and enterprise [5] platforms. Each skill carries a strict behavioral specification, stated in natural language: destructive actions demand confirmation, sensitive data must not leak, intermediate artifacts must be validated before release. Yet today’s deployments rest on a dangerous disconnect: these rules are documented, but the runtime merely trusts the agent to honor them. Nothing enforces the specification; the agent is left to police itself.

This blind trust is already failing in production. Zero-click prompt injections have exfiltrated corporate data from assistants such as Microsoft 365 Copilot [6] and Salesforce Agentforce [7], and an autonomous agent recently ran amok over a researcher’s inbox [8]. These incidents are instances of a broader class of specification violations: executions that use a skill in ways its declared contract forbids [9]. The stealthiest among them are not malformed commands that a syntax check would catch; they hide in the spaces between actions. An agent can execute a sequence of individually authorized, schema-valid tool calls that collectively break the specification.

Consider a multi-step perception pipeline, a standard architecture in autonomous driving systems [10], where policy dictates that any intermediate motion estimate must be validated before a downstream skill consumes it. An agent can produce a motion estimate MM, skip the validation step, and pass the unvalidated MM directly into a mask generator. In isolation, every tool call appears benign, and the final mask conforms to every schema check. Yet it is built on an artifact nobody verified, and it silently misleads the planner that decides how the vehicle moves. The violation is not a single bad action; it is an illicit data flow woven through the execution history. The example is grounded in a real SkillsBench execution [11]: the recorded run is benign-looking at the tool level, but violates the skill’s stated specification when checked as a trace. We return to it as our running example in Section III.

This temporal stealth exposes a structural blind spot in existing defenses. Sandboxes, resource boundaries, and governance layers confine files, credentials, processes, and network access [12, 13], but are blind to artifact-level obligations. Action-level monitors such as AgentSpec [14], Progent [15], Conseca [16], and PCAS [17] gate individual calls, yet lack the memory to enforce rules that span earlier events, value flows, or the identity of artifacts produced steps ago. Information-flow defenses confine what untrusted content may influence, but track taint rather than behavioral obligations [18, 19]. And LLM judges and trajectory analyzers [20, 21] see the whole run, but operate offline, without a deterministic verdict that can block a pending invocation in real time.

If a violation spans time and artifact identity, no single-call filter can see it. A defense must judge the observed trace in its entirety. Because the agent is untrusted, the specification’s meaning must be grounded independently of the agent’s own reasoning. And because hand-writing stateful monitors for a fast-growing skill ecosystem does not scale, natural-language specifications must be compiled into executable policies rather than encoded by hand. These requirements yield Vigil, a runtime reference monitor that enforces behavioral specifications over the live execution with no per-skill enforcement code.

Vigil targets finite observed traces and enforces finite-trace safety patterns such as precedence, response, absence, and artifact-binding obligations. It abstracts the agent’s raw tool calls into a finite trace of typed events with named arguments, outputs, and statuses. Crucially, Vigil does not map arbitrary temporal logic to a solver: its policies are finite-trace safety properties, and once grounded against the observed execution they unfold into quantifier-free satisfiability-modulo-theories (SMT) [22] constraints over trace facts. Each enforcement decision thus reduces to a single SMT query. On an inconsistency, the solver’s unsatisfiable core yields the offending invocation as a concrete witness (on the perception run above, the step that consumes the unvalidated estimate); Vigil blocks that invocation before its effects land, and the deployment can roll back, replan, or escalate to the user.

We evaluate Vigil on labeled real agent executions and on deployed real-world skill bundles. On 152 labeled runs drawn from SkillsBench [11] and Skill-Inject [23], Vigil detects the multi-step violations that bypass state-of-the-art action-boundary defenses such as AgentSpec [14] and Progent [15], leading the strongest baseline by 15.8 F1 points (95.8% recall at 89.6% precision); on the public AgentDojo [24] and SafeAgentBench [25] benchmarks it transfers with no per-benchmark tuning and ranks first on both. On 216 real-world skill-bundle executions from vendors including NVIDIA [5], Databricks [26], and Trail of Bits [27], Vigil surfaces 34 confirmed policy-violating runs, among them a composition-level specification defect in NVIDIA’s skill ecosystem that we disclosed and the maintainer acknowledged.

Contributions. We make the following contributions:

  • •

    A behavioral policy language with finite-trace temporal semantics. The language keeps the shape of an access-control rule but judges the whole execution, with temporal forms for the ordering and history conditions that per-request policies cannot state; its formal semantics fixes exactly when a run breaks a policy.

  • •

    The Vigil system: behavioral enforcement by SMT solving. An end-to-end runtime monitor grounds each policy in the run’s typed-event trace and reduces every enforcement decision to one SMT query, whose unsatisfiable core recovers the offending invocation whenever a policy is broken.

  • •

    Empirical evaluation on real agent runs. On 152 labeled runs [11, 23] and 216 real-world skill-bundle executions from NVIDIA [5], Anthropic [28], Trail of Bits [27], and others, Vigil reaches 95.8% recall at 89.6% precision and surfaces 34 confirmed violations, including an NVIDIA specification defect the maintainer has acknowledged.

II Background

Vigil builds on three established areas: the agent-skill execution model, reference-monitor theory, and the reduction of finite-trace temporal properties to SMT. We briefly recall each.

Agent skills. An LLM agent achieves operational reach by invoking skills [1] : packaged capabilities (e.g., file operations, cloud interactions, web access) that expose tools via standardized protocols such as MCP [29]. These skills typically ship with natural-language documentation defining tool schemas, permission boundaries, and usage constraints. These documents constitute the skill’s behavioral specification: the contract detailing what the agent is allowed to do and what preconditions must hold before sensitive effects occur. At runtime, the agent sequentially selects tools, supplies arguments, and consumes results, producing a finite sequence of tool calls known as the execution. Crucially, while the hosting environment can passively observe this execution, neither the agent driving the calls nor the unstructured inputs steering it can be trusted to adhere to the specification faithfully.

Reference monitors. The principled mechanism to constrain untrusted operations is a reference monitor: a trusted, unbypassable component that mediates security-relevant events and aborts any that violate a policy. Schneider’s seminal characterization establishes the theoretical limits of what such a monitor can enforce: specifically, safety properties recognizable by a security automaton observing the execution stream [30]. Later runtime-enforcement paradigms extend this response beyond mere halting [31]. Vigil instantiates a reference monitor in this lineage, lifted from individual actions to whole-trace temporal policies.

Temporal properties and SMT. The behavioral constraints dictated by skill specifications naturally manifest as temporal safety properties over the execution: an action is permitted only if preceded by a specific guard, an obligation must be satisfied before an artifact’s release, and forbidden data flows must never occur. These map directly to the precedence, response, and absence patterns well-established in finite-state verification [32], interpreted over finite traces [33]. Such properties can be decided by reduction to Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) [34]: while arbitrary temporal logic over infinite paths cannot be directly resolved by a solver, on a finite recorded trace a safety property unfolds into a quantifier-free ground formula. Any violation then manifests as an inconsistency with the trace’s facts, and the solver’s unsatisfiable core yields a precise, localized witness naming the events at fault [35]. This reduction underlies Vigil’s decision procedure.

III Overview

This section walks through a concrete run to show how a trace-level violation arises and how Vigil catches it at runtime.

III-A Motivating Example

We ground the problem in a single execution in which every step looks correct and the outcome is unsafe.

The scenario. Consider a critical autonomous-driving perception pipeline that processes dashcam video to generate moving-object masks. This is a highly safety-relevant workflow: the masks feed directly into the vehicle’s planning stack, and any pedestrian or vehicle they mislabel as static background is an obstacle the planner will fail to avoid. Because the camera itself moves with the vehicle, the agent must first estimate the camera’s own motion (egomotion) and compensate for it; the motion that remains reveals the independently moving objects.

Figure 1illustrates this scenario: the behavioral requirements (a), the four perception skills coordinating over shared artifacts (b), and an execution trajectory whose individually benign actions hide a trace-level violation (c).

The agent first invokes sampling-and-indexing at fps = 6, satisfying the task’s sampling rate invariant (R0). Next, it invokes egomotion-estimation, which tracks visual features and emits an intermediate camera-motion transform artifact, 𝙼\mathtt{M}. The downstream dyn-object-masks skill consumes 𝙼\mathtt{M} to warp the previous frame, isolate dynamic differences, and output the final mask; because the mask is computed only after this motion compensation, the ordering requirement (R2) is met. Finally, output-validation runs a schema checker on the generated mask before hand-off, fulfilling the requirement to validate outputs before release (R1).

However, the pipeline harbors a fatal flaw involving R3. The global composition policy demands that any intermediate artifact requiring validation must be explicitly validated before a downstream skill consumes it. In the violating trajectory (Figure 1c), the upstream skill produces 𝙼\mathtt{M}, and the downstream skill consumes that exact same 𝙼\mathtt{M}. Yet, no event validates 𝙼\mathtt{M} in between.

The consequence is insidious: the final mask satisfies every JSON schema check, so the system accepts the output as a success. But because it is built upon an unchecked motion estimate 𝙼\mathtt{M}, the mask is semantically wrong, and the planner inherits the error. The violation leaves no trace in any single command. It is woven into the negative space of the execution history: a critical validation event that simply never happened.

The challenges. This temporal stealth exposes why traditional, single-call defenses fail: the violation exists in the semantic gap between an abstract human rule and the messy reality of an agent’s execution trace. Bridging this gap introduces three fundamental challenges.

C1: Contextual specification. The requirement “validate an artifact before consumption” (R3) does not dictate a fixed API call: in this run the artifact happens to be 𝙼\mathtt{M}, the producer is egomotion-estimation, and the consumer is dyn-object-masks; in another run all three differ. A stateless monitor cannot enforce a rule that must reshape itself around what the agent did three steps ago.

C2: Policy semantics from raw execution. Even with the policy contextualized, raw execution logs are semantically opaque. A command writing a matrix to disk is raw data; the monitor must elevate it to the policy-level fact that 𝙼\mathtt{M} was produced, and must recognize that the final CSR schema checker validates the mask, not the intermediate 𝙼\mathtt{M}. Chaotic tool calls must become a typed, factual history.

C3: Agent-independent enforcement. An agent focused on finishing the task can conflate the final CSR validation with the validation 𝙼\mathtt{M} requires, convincing itself that R3 is satisfied. The agent is also the very entity under attack (e.g., via prompt injection), so its interpretation of the rules is untrusted: the runtime needs an independent authority that evaluates the trace deterministically.

III-B Vigil: Trace-Grounded Enforcement

Vigil resolves these challenges by operating as an end-to-end runtime reference monitor. The key insight driving its design, and the thread connecting the solutions to C1, C2, and C3, is the strict separation of a behavioral specification’s generic meaning from its run-specific instantiation. Vigil achieves this by grounding abstract specification terms to concrete artifacts, preserving cross-call identity through value bindings, and checking finite-trace temporal obligations before allowing any pending action to proceed.

Figure 2illustrates this architecture. When the untrusted agent initiates a pending tool invocation (e.g., the mask generation step), the runtime intercepts it and performs a deterministic, four-step verification lifecycle:

  1. 1.

    Trace Abstraction: A trusted collector provides the trace prefix (the sequence of all actions taken so far). Vigil parses these raw tool calls into strongly typed events, recovering the data flow and artifact identities (e.g., tracking the specific transform 𝙼\mathtt{M}).

  2. 2.

    Policy Grounding: The abstract, natural-language behavioral specification is instantiated against these concrete trace facts. The contextual rule “validate before consumption” dynamically becomes an exact, executable constraint over the artifact 𝙼\mathtt{M}.

  3. 3.

    SMT Check: Vigil formulates the pending invocation and the grounded policy as a Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) query, deciding whether allowing the pending action would break the execution’s temporal contract.

  4. 4.

    Intervention: If the solver’s verdict is safe, the action executes. If unsafe, Vigil blocks the invocation. The solver’s unsatisfiable core extracts a localized witness (here, that 𝙼\mathtt{M} was consumed without validation), allowing the deployment environment to trigger a rollback, replan the workflow, or escalate to a human.

The following sections formalize this lifecycle. Section IV details how raw executions are abstracted into trace facts (C2). Section V then defines the behavioral policy language (C1) and the agent-independent SMT reduction with witness localization (C3).

III-C Threat Model

Vigil defends a user who delegates work to an agent that invokes third-party skills, each expected to stay within its declared specification. The adversary controls skill content and any document the agent reads, and plants a prompt injection that steers an otherwise-benign skill outside that scope, to exfiltrate data, delete files, or escalate privilege. The agent and the skill code it runs are therefore untrusted: the agent is the very component the attacker subverts.

Vigil sits outside this boundary. It observes the execution through a trusted collector that records the agent’s tool calls in a sandbox, and decides policies with a trusted SMT solver over an operator-authored specification. The collector is assumed complete: behavior that never surfaces as a tool call, such as computation inside an opaque script, lies outside the recorded trace and outside Vigil’s view.

III-D Problem Statement

With the trust boundary fixed, the problem Vigil decides can be stated. An agent run is given as a finite trace τ\tau of its tool-call events, in the order they occurred; the behavioral requirements of its skill specification are given as a policy PP over that trace. The trace records what the run did, and the policy states what it must do, with rules on the order of events and on the values that flow between them.

A policy P={φ1,…,φm}P=\{\varphi_{1},\dots,\varphi_{m}\} is a finite set of statements, and the trace must obey every one. We write τ⊧φ\tau\models\varphi when the trace satisfies a statement, and τ⊧P\tau\models P when it satisfies them all. The checking problem is to decide, given a trace τ\tau and a policy PP, whether τ⊧P\tau\models P. Deployed online, Vigil poses this problem over the trace recorded so far: a failed prohibition or precondition blocks the pending call, and an obligation that waits on a later step is judged when the run ends (Section VI).

IV The Vigil Framework

The problem is now fixed: decide whether a trace τ\tau satisfies a policy PP. Neither input arrives in that form: an execution is a stream of tool calls of many shapes, and its requirements begin as natural language naming different objects and steps from one execution to the next. Vigil closes both gaps with a single idea: read everything the check needs off the run itself.

Figure 3lays out the three stages over two inputs: the agent’s execution LL and the specification DD. Abstract reads the execution once and produces the two objects the later stages share: the fact base ⟦τ⟧\llbracket\tau\rrbracket records what the run did, and the signature Σ\Sigma collects the actions, argument names, and values the run exhibited. Compile then turns the specification into a policy PP phrased in that same vocabulary, so every requirement is anchored to symbols the run actually produced. Finally, Verify tests each statement of PP against ⟦τ⟧\llbracket\tau\rrbracket and reports the run safe when all hold, or unsafe with the offending events.

The framework thus rests on two components: an abstraction that makes the behavior checkable, and a policy language in which requirements are stated and decided. Section IV-A states the procedure; the rest of this section develops the abstraction, and Section V the language.

IV-A Algorithm Overview

Algorithm 1makes the procedure precise: two preprocessing stages, then a loop that puts the compiled policy through the solver one statement at a time. Reading it line by line fixes what each stage must deliver; the sections that follow fill in the details.

Lines 4–5 are the two preprocessing stages of Figure 3: Abstract (line 4) yields the signature Σ\Sigma and the fact base ⟦τ⟧\llbracket\tau\rrbracket, and Compile (line 5) phrases the policy PP in Σ\Sigma.

Lines 6–10 verify the policy one statement at a time; line 6 starts from an empty witness set WW. For each statement φ\varphi, line 8 encodes it into its requirement ℛφ\mathcal{R}_{\varphi}: the formula that holds exactly when the trace complies. Line 9 then puts a single question to the solver: do the facts refute the requirement? If 𝗎𝗇𝗌𝖺𝗍⁡(⟦τ⟧∧ℛφ){\sf unsat}(\llbracket\tau\rrbracket\wedge\mathcal{R}_{\varphi}), the recorded run breaks φ\varphi; otherwise it meets it. On a violation, line 10 localizes the offending events as loc⁡(φ)\mathrm{loc}(\varphi), read from the solver’s unsatisfiable core, and records the pair (φ,loc⁡(φ))(\varphi,\mathrm{loc}(\varphi)); because statements are checked independently, every witness is tied to the one statement that failed.

Lines 11–12 return the verdict, and with it the answer to the checking problem: safe when WW is empty (every statement held, τ⊧P\tau\models P), and unsafe otherwise. WW reports both the broken statements and where they broke.

IV-B From Calls to Checkable Facts

We now develop the framework’s first component: the abstraction computed by Abstract. A run arrives as nothing more than a stream of tool calls. The abstraction turns it into the object the check needs: a typed, ordered trace of what the run did, and a closed-world account of what a policy may say about it. Both are read off the run itself, so they are fixed by the execution rather than declared in advance.

Typed events. A run’s calls come in many shapes: the same file read may arrive as a shell command, as a dedicated tool call, or as one field of a larger request, and each spells its arguments differently. A policy should turn on none of this, since it speaks of reading a file, not of any one syntax for it. Abstract therefore collapses every call to a single typed event, the record of the four things a policy can name,

e=⟨a⁡(e),e⁡[⋅],s⁡(e),o⁡(e)⟩:e\;=\;\big\langle\;a(e),\;\;e[\cdot],\;\;s(e),\;\;o(e)\;\big\rangle:

its action a⁡(e)a(e), a partial map e⁡[⋅]e[\cdot] sending each argument name k∈dom⁡(e)k\in\mathrm{dom}(e) to its value e⁡[k]e[k], a status s⁡(e)∈{⊤,⊥}s(e)\in\{\top,\bot\} (success or error), and a bounded observation o⁡(e)o(e) of the output.

Two choices in this record matter for policies. First, arguments are keyed by name rather than position, so a policy can name the file a step reads without knowing how the call was written. Second, the output is kept only as a bounded observation; that suffices to test o⁡(e)≈po(e)\approx p against a pattern pp without asking the solver to reason over unbounded data. Because the same typed events describe every skill, one decision procedure checks them all, with no per-skill code.

The ordered trace. The violations we care about turn on when things happen: a step that must run before another, a value used after the point where it should have been checked. Abstract therefore keeps the events in execution order, as a trace

τ=e1≺e2≺⋯,\tau\;=\;e_{1}\prec e_{2}\prec\cdots,

and we write e′≻ee^{\prime}\succ e for e≺e′e\prec e^{\prime}. The typed record and the order together capture what ran, with what arguments, and in what sequence. One piece remains: fixing what a policy may say about the run, and the facts it is judged on.

Closed-world grounding. A requirement also turns on what did not happen: a prohibition holds only if the forbidden step never occurred, and a precondition is breached exactly when the guard is missing. Deciding an absence is sound only if the record is complete. Vigil therefore treats the trace as a closed world. The run fixes two things: the vocabulary a policy may use, which keeps every condition finite, and the complete set of facts the policy is judged against, which makes absences decisive.

Definition 1 (Signature and facts).

Let EE be the events of τ\tau. The signature Σ=(A,K,V)\Sigma=(A,K,V) collects the actions, argument names, and values the run exhibits,

A\displaystyle A ={a(e)∣e∈E},K=⋃e∈Edom(e),\displaystyle=\{\,a(e)\mid e\in E\,\},\qquad K=\textstyle\bigcup_{e\in E}\mathrm{dom}(e),
V\displaystyle V ={e⁡[k]∣e∈E∧k∈dom⁡(e)}∪{o⁡(e)∣e∈E},\displaystyle=\{\,e[k]\mid e\in E\wedge k\in\mathrm{dom}(e)\,\}\cup\{\,o(e)\mid e\in E\,\},

and the fact base ⟦τ⟧\llbracket\tau\rrbracket reads the trace out field by field as a set of ground atoms,

⟦τ⟧=\displaystyle\llbracket\tau\rrbracket\;= ⋃e∈E({a⁡(e),s⁡(e),o⁡(e)}∪{e⁡[k]∣k∈dom⁡(e)})\displaystyle\bigcup_{e\in E}\Big(\{\,a(e),\ s(e),\ o(e)\,\}\cup\{\,e[k]\mid k\in\mathrm{dom}(e)\,\}\Big)
∪{ei≺ej∣i<j},\displaystyle}{\displaystyle\cup\ \{\,e_{i}\prec e_{j}\mid i<j\,\},

where each field stands for the equality fixing its value, for instance a⁡(e)=warpAffinea(e)=\text{{warpAffine}}.

The fact base is complete for the run: an atom missing from ⟦τ⟧\llbracket\tau\rrbracket records something the run did not do, so verdicts that rest on absences are sound. Its constants are the run’s concrete literals, so distinct names or values never coincide, and a condition on an argument an event does not carry is false. Every atom names the event it records, so a violation found over these facts traces back to the exact events at fault.

Example 1 (Abstracting the running example).

For the dashcam run the signature is small:

A⊇{estimate_M,warpAffine,validate_output},A\supseteq\{\text{{estimate\_M}},\text{{warpAffine}},\text{{validate\_output}}\},

with argument names like transform, target, and file in KK, and the values that pass between steps in VV. One of those values is the fitted transform 𝙼\mathtt{M}: the egomotion step e3e_{3} records it as output, and the warp step e5e_{5} takes it as input, so among the few dozen atoms of ⟦τ⟧\llbracket\tau\rrbracket are

o⁡(e3)=𝙼,e5​[transform]=𝙼,e3≺e5.o(e_{3})=\mathtt{M},\qquad e_{5}[\text{{transform}}]=\mathtt{M},\qquad e_{3}\prec e_{5}.

Requirement R3 (validate an artifact before consuming it) is now a question of order: is there a validating event for 𝙼\mathtt{M} earlier than e5e_{5}? The closed world lets a verdict rest on absences: the run performs no network call, so ⟦τ⟧\llbracket\tau\rrbracket contains no such atom, and a prohibition on network egress is judged satisfied by that absence, not by assumption.

With the run reduced to this fact base and signature, the only remaining piece is the policy checked against them; Section V defines that language and its reduction to an SMT query.

V Behavioral Policy Language

This section develops the language in which the recorded behavior is checked: a policy lifts the familiar access-control rule from a single request to the whole trace. We give its syntax (Section V-A), the compilation of statements to requirements over the fact base (Section V-B), and the satisfiability check that decides them with localized witnesses (Section V-C).

V-A Stating Policies

Behavioral requirements vary in wording, but they place three recurring demands on a rule. It has to pick out the steps it concerns; it has to constrain their order, since an obligation typically demands one step before another; and it often has to tie two steps to the same value, so that a guard counts only when it covered what a later step consumes. Figure 4 gives a language with one construct for each: a pattern selects single events, a temporal form relates one or two patterns by their order, and a variable xx ties two patterns to the same value. A statement is one form applied to its patterns. In access-control terms, a statement is a rule over an action, a resource, and a condition, but its only effect is to flag a violation, never to allow or deny. We take the constructs in turn and close with a fallback for requirements the forms do not cover.

Patterns. A pattern selects the events a statement concerns. It is a conjunction of conditions on one event:

  • •

    a∈αa\in\alpha constrains the action: the event is one of the kinds of step in α\alpha.

  • •

    k∈Sk\in S and k∼pk\sim p constrain an argument: the value under name kk lies in the set SS, or matches the text pattern pp.

  • •

    k=xk=x pins an argument to the variable xx; a statement uses xx once in each of its two patterns.

  • •

    o∼po\sim p constrains the output: the recorded output matches the text pattern pp.

  • •

    s=⊤s=\top and s=⊥s=\bot constrain the status: the step succeeded or failed.

  • •

    ψ∧ψ′\psi\wedge\psi^{\prime} combines conditions.

A pattern’s symbols come from the run’s signature Σ=(A,K,V)\Sigma=(A,K,V): α⊆A\alpha\subseteq A is a set of the run’s actions, S⊆VS\subseteq V a set of its values, and k∈Kk\in K one of its argument names. A pattern can therefore name only what the run exhibits; a term of the specification with no counterpart in Σ\Sigma denotes the empty set, and a condition on it is false. The matching ∼\sim is plain text matching; it is evaluated outside the solver, and the solver sees only its ground outcomes e⁡[k]≈pe[k]\approx p.

Example 2 (Patterns on the running example).

R3 governs the steps that consume a transform; on the dashcam run these are the frame warps. One conjunction selects them:

ψc=(a∈{warpAffine})∧(s=⊤).\psi_{c}\;=\;(a\in\{\text{{warpAffine}}\})\wedge(s=\top).

It matches every warp step that succeeded. A second pattern selects the hand-off of a mask:

ψh=(a∈{release_artifact})∧(file∼"*.csr"),\psi_{h}\;=\;(a\in\{\text{{release\_artifact}}\})\wedge(\text{{file}}\sim\text{{"*.csr"}}),

where ∼\sim compares the argument’s text against the pattern, so ψh\psi_{h} covers every CSR file the run might name (out_0.csr, out_1.csr, …) without enumerating them.

Temporal forms. A pattern selects events; the temporal form constrains their order. The six forms name the ordering and history conditions that recur in behavioral requirements:

  • •

    𝖺𝖻𝗌⁡(ψ){\sf abs}(\psi) demands the absence of ψ\psi: a flat prohibition.

  • •

    𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖼⁡(ψ,ψ′){\sf prec}(\psi,\psi^{\prime}) gives ψ′\psi^{\prime} precedence: ψ\psi is allowed only after ψ′\psi^{\prime} has happened (the shape of a precondition).

  • •

    𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗉⁡(ψ,ψ′){\sf resp}(\psi,\psi^{\prime}) is the dual: it requires a later response ψ′\psi^{\prime} to every ψ\psi (an obligation).

  • •

    𝖻𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗉ℓ​(ψ,ψ′){\sf bresp}_{\ell}(\psi,\psi^{\prime}) bounds that response to the next ℓ\ell events.

  • •

    𝗋𝗌𝗅𝗏⁡(ψ,ψ′){\sf rslv}(\psi,\psi^{\prime}) requires every ψ\psi to be resolved by the end of the run: only the finally delivered state is judged, and a later ψ\psi supersedes an earlier one.

  • •

    𝗎𝗇𝗍𝗂𝗅⁡(ψ,ψ′,ψb){\sf until}(\psi,\psi^{\prime},\psi_{b}) guards an interval: after a trigger ψ\psi, the bad pattern ψb\psi_{b} is forbidden until a resolving ψ′\psi^{\prime} intervenes.

Example 3 (Forms of the running example).

The dashcam requirements translate form by form. R2 requires masks only after global motion compensation; it is a precedence between two action patterns:

𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖼⁡(a∈{emit_mask},a∈{warpAffine}).{\sf prec}\big(\,a\in\{\text{{emit\_mask}}\},\;\;a\in\{\text{{warpAffine}}\}\,\big).

R1 requires validation before hand-off; it is a precedence on the hand-off pattern ψh\psi_{h} above:

𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖼⁡(ψh,a∈{validate_output}).{\sf prec}\big(\,\psi_{h},\;\;a\in\{\text{{validate\_output}}\}\,\big).

R0 fixes the sampling rate; it is the absence (𝖺𝖻𝗌{\sf abs}) of any off-specification rate. Finally, R3 requires a validation-required artifact to be validated before it is consumed; it ties two steps to the same value:

𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖼⁡(ψc∧(transform=x),ψv∧(target=x)),{\sf prec}\big(\,\psi_{c}\wedge(\text{{transform}}=x),\;\;\psi_{v}\wedge(\text{{target}}=x)\,\big),

where ψv=(a∈{validate_output})\psi_{v}=(a\in\{\text{{validate\_output}}\}) matches the validating steps. ψc\psi_{c} selects the warp steps, transform=x\text{{transform}}=x names the value a warp consumes, and target=x\text{{target}}=x requires the validated value to be that same one. On the dashcam run xx is the transform 𝙼\mathtt{M}: the statement is broken exactly when a warp consumes 𝙼\mathtt{M} with no earlier validate of 𝙼\mathtt{M}.

Beyond the six forms. For a requirement that none of the forms expresses, a statement applies □\Box (“always”) directly to a temporal body Θ\Theta: patterns combined with ¬\neg, ∧\wedge, ◇−\Diamond^{-} (“at some earlier point”), and ◇+\Diamond^{+} (“at some later point”); the two diamonds are past- and future-directed shorthands for the standard eventually operator ◇\Diamond. Appendix E writes out this reading for each preset form.

V-B Compiling Statements into Requirements

A statement says what must hold; to test it against a trace, we need a formula the solver can check. Compilation is syntax-directed, from a policy down to its patterns: Vigil compiles each statement φ\varphi of the policy to its requirement ℛφ\mathcal{R}_{\varphi} through the judgment

Σ⊢φ↝ℛφ,\Sigma\vdash\varphi\rightsquigarrow\mathcal{R}_{\varphi},

read “under signature Σ\Sigma, statement φ\varphi compiles to requirement ℛφ\mathcal{R}_{\varphi}”, also written 𝖾𝗇𝖼𝗈𝖽𝖾⁡(φ,Σ){\sf encode}(\varphi,\Sigma); Figure 5 gives the rules.

The figure has three parts. At the top, Policy conjoins the statements’ requirements: a policy holds exactly when every statement does. The remaining rules build ℛφ\mathcal{R}_{\varphi}, one per form plus Fallback, and they share one shape: a guarded quantification over the events. The outer conjunction ranges over all events, and for an event matching ψ\psi the body requires a matching ψ′\psi^{\prime} at the right position in ≺\prec (earlier for 𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖼{\sf prec}, later for 𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗉{\sf resp}, within the next ℓ\ell events for 𝖻𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗉{\sf bresp}, written e≺ℓe′e\prec_{\ell}e^{\prime}, and so on). The foot interprets the leaves: each pattern denotes a one-event predicate ψ⁡(e)\psi(e), and each temporal-body operator unfolds into the same finite quantification.

A requirement is therefore one condition per event, conjoined; writing ℛφ​(e)\mathcal{R}_{\varphi}(e) for the condition on event ee,

ℛφ=⋀e∈Eℛφ​(e).\mathcal{R}_{\varphi}\;=\;\bigwedge_{e\in E}\mathcal{R}_{\varphi}(e).

For 𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖼{\sf prec}, ℛφ​(e)\mathcal{R}_{\varphi}(e) reads: if ee matches ψ\psi, then some earlier event matches ψ′\psi^{\prime}; when the two patterns share the variable xx, each disjunct of a binary form gains the conjunct e′​[k′]=e⁡[k]e^{\prime}[k^{\prime}]=e[k], so only the events that agree count. Every quantifier ranges over the finite event set EE, and every set is drawn from the finite signature, so each ℛφ\mathcal{R}_{\varphi} is a ground, quantifier-free formula over ⟦τ⟧\llbracket\tau\rrbracket, decided by an ordinary solver query.

V-C Deciding Requirements with Witnesses

Checking a statement is a single solver query: the recorded facts either are consistent with the requirement or refute it, and on a refutation the offending events are read off the solver’s unsatisfiable core.

Encoding. Vigil asserts the fact base ⟦τ⟧\llbracket\tau\rrbracket together with the requirement, one condition ℛφ​(e)\mathcal{R}_{\varphi}(e) per event, and asks whether the facts refute the requirement:

𝗎𝗇𝗌𝖺𝗍(⟦τ⟧∧ℛφ)⇔τ⊧̸φ.{\sf unsat}\big(\llbracket\tau\rrbracket\wedge\mathcal{R}_{\varphi}\big)\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\tau\not\models\varphi.

The equivalence holds because the fact base is complete: the facts fix everything the run did, so they contradict ℛφ\mathcal{R}_{\varphi} exactly when the run breaks one of its conditions. Because ⟦τ⟧\llbracket\tau\rrbracket pins down a finite structure and ℛφ\mathcal{R}_{\varphi} is quantifier-free over it, the query is decidable. The checking problem thus reduces statement by statement,

τ⊧̸P⇔⋁φ∈P𝗎𝗇𝗌𝖺𝗍(⟦τ⟧∧ℛφ),\tau\not\models P\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\bigvee_{\varphi\in P}{\sf unsat}\big(\llbracket\tau\rrbracket\wedge\mathcal{R}_{\varphi}\big),

and the goal fixed by the problem statement is decided by mm such queries over one fact base: the run satisfies PP exactly when no query is unsatisfiable.

Localization. An inconsistency establishes that the run is unsafe, but an operator acting on the verdict also needs to know where it broke. The solver reports more than 𝗎𝗇𝗌𝖺𝗍{\sf unsat}. 𝗆𝗎𝖼{\sf muc} returns a minimal unsatisfiable core: a smallest set of asserted conditions that already contradicts the facts. Each condition in the core names the event it constrains, so localization is a lookup rather than a search:

loc⁡(φ)={e∈E∣ℛφ​(e)∈𝗆𝗎𝖼⁡(⟦τ⟧∧ℛφ)},\mathrm{loc}(\varphi)\;=\;\{\,e\in E\mid\mathcal{R}_{\varphi}(e)\in{\sf muc}(\llbracket\tau\rrbracket\wedge\mathcal{R}_{\varphi})\,\},

and one solver query yields the verdict and its core together. For the binary forms, the core names an event matching ψ\psi whose required ψ′\psi^{\prime} is missing; for 𝖺𝖻𝗌{\sf abs} it names an event exhibiting ψ\psi, and for 𝗎𝗇𝗍𝗂𝗅{\sf until} it names the trigger of the broken interval.

Example 4 (Localizing the violation).

On the violating dashcam run, the warp step e5e_{5} consumes the transform 𝙼\mathtt{M}. The condition that R3’s requirement places on e5e_{5} asks for an earlier validate of the value it consumes:

ℛφ​(e5)=ψc​(e5)⇒\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\varphi}(e_{5})\;=\;\psi_{c}(e_{5})\Rightarrow{}
⋁e′≺e5(ψv​(e′)∧e′​[target]CLOSE\displaystyle\bigvee_{e^{\prime}\prec e_{5}}\big(\psi_{v}(e^{\prime})\wedge e^{\prime}[\text{{target}}] OPEN=e5​[transform]).\displaystyle=e_{5}[\text{{transform}}]\big).

The facts make ψc​(e5)\psi_{c}(e_{5}) true and fix e5​[transform]=𝙼e_{5}[\text{{transform}}]=\mathtt{M}, but no event before e5e_{5} validates 𝙼\mathtt{M}, so every disjunct is false: the facts and ℛφ​(e5)\mathcal{R}_{\varphi}(e_{5}) cannot hold together, and the query is unsatisfiable. Every other condition is consistent with the facts, so 𝗆𝗎𝖼{\sf muc} returns the singleton {ℛφ​(e5)}\{\mathcal{R}_{\varphi}(e_{5})\}, and the lookup gives loc⁡(φ)={e5}\mathrm{loc}(\varphi)=\{e_{5}\}. Vigil surfaces e5e_{5} as the action to block.

VI Implementation

We implement Vigil in roughly 7,000 lines of Python 3.12 as a prototype of the framework in Figure 3. The implementation uses Z3 as the backend SMT solver and claude-opus-4-6 for the specification-compilation step (Appendix C), with fast-mode. The language model is used only to draft statements in the policy language; all grounding, validation, SMT encoding, and safe/unsafe decisions are performed by deterministic components. Two implementation choices keep the language model contained. First, in Compile the model may only use the vocabulary that Abstract recovers from the run, and a statement it proposes is accepted only after validation against the observed signature; clauses that cannot be grounded are reported as unsupported rather than silently kept. Second, Verify invokes Z3 on each grounded statement independently and reports a witness per statement, so localization stays tied to the statement that failed. For argument grounding, Compile can only reference parameter roles that Abstract binds to concrete trace events. Vigil grounds these roles from a small catalog of common POSIX and developer-tool commands, AST-based recovery for case-shipped Python, shell, and JavaScript scripts, and optional --help probing for external CLIs. --help probing is opt-in because it runs the target binary.

Deployment. Vigil runs outside the agent, in a sandboxed or mediated runtime that records the execution stream and can pause policy-relevant operations before their effects are released; this fits agent workflows that already mediate tool execution through a workspace, sandbox, or gateway. At each enforcement point, the runtime presents Vigil with the trace so far and the pending operation. Prohibitions and preconditions are decided on the trace so far, since a witnessed violation cannot be undone; open obligations are judged when the run ends.

Enforcement actions. On a violating pending invocation, the runtime’s pre-execution hook denies the call and returns the localized witness (Claude Code’s pre-tool-use deny, or an MCP gateway holding a request); a blocked call has no effects to undo. The deployment then halts the run, asks for user approval, or rolls the sandbox back to its last checkpoint and lets the agent replan: Vigil decides whether the pending operation is safe, and the deployment chooses how to proceed. In the real-world study (Section VII-E), external CLIs are replaced by logging stubs, so verdicts gate the trace replay rather than live effects.

VII Evaluation

In this section, we present the design and results of the evaluation for answering the following research questions:

  • •

    RQ1 (Effectiveness). How effectively does Vigil detect specification violations in real LLM-agent trajectories without flagging benign workloads, compared with state-of-the-art runtime defenses?

  • •

    RQ2 (Ablation). What is the contribution of Vigil’s individual components?

  • •

    RQ3 (Runtime Overhead). What is the per-case cost of Vigil, and how does it scale with the length of the trajectory?

  • •

    RQ4 (Real-world Study). Does Vigil detect and block policy violations in real-world skill deployments?

VII-A Experimental Setup

Our evaluation rests on a labeled corpus of real agent executions, each paired with its skill specification and a ground-truth violation label, against which we compare Vigil with a set of runtime-enforcement baselines.

Benchmark. We construct the main evaluation set from SkillsBench [11] and Skill-Inject [23], combining them into a final labeled evaluation set, denoted SB+SI. This set contains 152 executions: 72 policy-violating trajectories and 80 benign trajectories. We use AgentDojo [24] and SafeAgentBench [25] only for additional cross-benchmark comparisons. Further details on labeling are in Appendix A.

  • •

    SkillsBench. SkillsBench provides over 4,000 task-performance trajectories. We use an LLM to screen for trajectories whose skill documentation states an enforceable behavioral policy and whose execution appears relevant to that policy. We then manually inspect each candidate to label whether it violates or follows the policy.

  • •

    Skill-Inject. It does not provide raw execution trajectories, we replay its tasks in Claude Code using claude-sonnet-4-6 with bypassPermissions, then record the resulting agent executions. From these replayed executions, we identify and label trajectories that violate the behavioral policy stated by the skill and trajectories that do not.

  • •

    Additional comparisons. AgentDojo is a dynamic benchmark for prompt-injection attacks and defenses in tool-using LLM agents, and SafeAgentBench evaluates safe task planning in embodied LLM agents. We use both as cross-benchmark comparisons under the settings used by the corresponding baselines. For AgentDojo, we use the published trajectories generated by gpt-4o-2024-05-13.

Baselines. We select three direct baselines to represent the prevailing paradigms in agent policy enforcement:

  • •

    AgentSpec [14] represents action-boundary enforcement. Its rule language can state temporal triggers, but each rule is evaluated when its trigger action is proposed, so the decision sees one pending action at a time and cannot reach evidence that lives elsewhere in the trace, such as artifact identity or long-range event order.

  • •

    Progent [15] similarly represents action-boundary guardrails, compiling policies into per-tool-call permission allowlists.

  • •

    LLM-as-judge uses claude-opus-4-6 as a model-only whole-trace judge. It observes the full trace context, but operates without deterministic formal semantics and cannot produce a reliable, localized witness for runtime blocking.

Together, these baselines allow us to compare Vigil’s trace-grounded approach against both localized and informal enforcement strategies. For AgentSpec and Progent, we count a blocked action as a reported violation; for LLM-as-judge, we count a positive judgment as a reported violation (Appendix B).

Metrics. For violation detection, we report TP, FP, precision, recall, and F1 per system; any reported violation on a benign trace counts as a false positive. For overhead, we report end-to-end latency and stage-level latency.

Experiment settings. We ran all experiments on a server running Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS with 16 logical Intel Xeon Gold 5222 CPUs and 125 GiB of RAM.

VII-B RQ1. Effectiveness

We evaluate Vigil, AgentSpec, Progent, and the LLM-as-judge baseline on SB+SI. Each system receives the same specification-derived policy and execution trace, and we score whether it reports a policy violation under its intended enforcement interface. Representative policy categories and formalizations for SB+SI appear in Appendix D.

Overall results. Table I compares Vigil with the baselines and shows a stark contrast between benchmarks that require trace-level reasoning and those decided by single-call.

On our primary target, SB+SI, where violations turn on temporal structure and value binding, Vigil detects 69 of the 72 violating executions with only 8 false positives on 80 benign runs (92.6% F1). Action-boundary defenses cannot track historical artifacts or prerequisites: AgentSpec and Progent miss about half the violations (57.6% and 50.3% F1). The LLM-as-judge baseline sees the full context and does better (76.8% F1), but still misses 24 temporal violations for lack of formal grounding. Vigil leads the strongest baseline by 15.8 F1 points.

The AgentDojo and SafeAgentBench rows serve as cross-benchmark sanity checks. Their labeled violations are largely visible at a single action boundary (e.g., a prohibited command string), exactly what AgentSpec and Progent are optimized for. AgentDojo also contains semantic prompt-injection conflicts that a strong whole-trace judge such as claude-opus-4-6 can often classify directly. Even so, Vigil holds its own without per-benchmark tuning: it is the strongest system on both SafeAgentBench (96.3% vs 96.0% F1) and AgentDojo (94.2% vs 94.1% F1), albeit by narrow margins. SB+SI remains the setting that measures the trace-level violations Vigil is built for.

These results reflect enforcement granularity. The same bash call may be benign or violating depending on the file it targets, an earlier validation, and the artifact it leaves behind; Vigil improves recall by deciding over grounded events across the full trace rather than at the pending action alone.

Measuring enforcement reliability. A runtime monitor fails in exactly two ways: it misses a real violation, or it falsely blocks a benign run. Either error can be hidden by accepting more of the other: flag everything and recall is perfect, flag nothing and false alarms vanish. Figure 6 therefore reports the one number that punishes both, the balanced enforcement error (BEE):

BEE=12​(FNR+FPR),\mathrm{BEE}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,\big(\mathrm{FNR}+\mathrm{FPR}\big),

where the FNR\mathrm{FNR} is the fraction of violating executions a system misses and the FPR\mathrm{FPR} is the fraction of benign executions flagged; BEE is the complement of balanced accuracy. Thus, BEE is how often the monitor gets the call wrong, counting a missed violation and a blocked legitimate run as equally costly. We macro-average over the three benchmark sets so each counts equally. Vigil attains the lowest macro BEE (5.4%), less than half that of the next best complete baseline: reducing both error types rather than optimizing recall alone.

Error analysis. The baselines err in different directions. Progent over-blocks benign executions because it turns the policy into a narrow allowlist: SB+SI policies rarely enumerate every safe command, path, or argument, and all 47 of its false positives are benign calls the allowlist rejects. The LLM-as-judge errs the other way, missing 24 violations. Vigil avoids both by checking grounded trace events rather than a complete allowlist or an unconstrained model verdict.

Vigil’s own remaining errors mark two system boundaries. False negatives mark the boundary of trace observability: policy-relevant evidence can stay hidden inside an opaque utility script. In Figure 7a, the agent invokes secure_archive.py; the script creates an unencrypted ZIP (a no-op zf.setpassword) and immediately unlinks the source file. The policy requires an integrity check between write and deletion, but both actions run inside the script body and never surface as trace events.

False positives mark the boundary of compilation fidelity: the LLM can translate a specification into an overly broad statement or a wrong temporal form. In Figure 7b, the specification limits a rule to bulk calendar modifications, the generated statement drops the qualifier, and the monitor fires on a benign single-event reschedule. In these cases, the error is semantic over-generalization, not a failure to compile. Both boundaries define clear future work: deeper sandbox instrumentation, and stricter compilation prompting.

VII-C RQ2. Ablation Study

We ablate the two structures that make operation understanding available before solver checking. All variants use the same SB+SI evaluation set, labels, and metrics as RQ1, and each removes one source of structure while leaving the rest of the pipeline unchanged:

  1. 1.

    w/o Argument Grounding removes the grounding of command and script arguments into event fields, so the monitor still observes tool calls but loses which values within an event can be referenced by the policy.

  2. 2.

    w/o Policy Structure removes the structured intermediate form used when translating natural-language specifications into executable policies, testing whether the compilation step preserves ordering constraints, object identities, and final-state obligations without that.

Table IIreports the ablation results. Removing argument grounding reduces precision by 11.6 percentage points and recall by 31.9 points. Without grounded arguments, Compile cannot connect conditions to the values that matter within an event, so the monitor falls back to action-only matches that miss most argument-dependent violations. The missed cases are concentrated in protocols whose violation depends on the meaning of command arguments, such as paths, modes, script targets, payload strings, or target objects. Removing policy structure reduces precision by 2.9 percentage points and recall by 5.5 points. The compiler still produces executable statements, but more often emits broad single-event 𝖺𝖻𝗌{\sf abs} statements that miss temporal/final-state violations or fire on benign payloads that match the generated condition. These misses are concentrated in protocols whose natural-language form is not a simple forbidden action, including ordering constraints, prerequisite checks, and final-artifact requirements. Together, the ablations show that Vigil depends on structured evidence before solver checking: grounded event values and policy structure.

VII-D RQ3. Runtime Overhead

We measure Vigil’s overhead on all SB+SI traces and decompose end-to-end latency into the three stages in Figure 3. Table IV shows that Vigil averages 4.38 s per trace, with Compile’s single LLM call accounting for 92.5%.

This cost does not grow with trace length. Compile’s input is the observed vocabulary of the run, and Figure 8 shows it saturating near 10 KB once the initial events have introduced the run’s tools, argument names, and artifact types; end-to-end runtime therefore stays stable across the full range of trace lengths.

For modern AI coding-agent workloads, where standard Bash commands average 4–6 s and tasks run for several minutes [39], a 4-second overhead is well within acceptable limits. More importantly, because the bottleneck is entirely within the LLM translation step rather than the SMT solver, it is highly optimizable. Deployments can cache compiled policies per skill, utilize faster model serving, or deploy small local distilled models to reduce end-to-end latency, while the determinism of the sub-second Verify path remains uncompromised.

VII-E RQ4. Real-world Skill-Bundle Study

To assess Vigil in the real world, we evaluate it on skill bundles drawn from deployed ecosystems. We deployed Vigil over 216 executions sampled across three tiers: default-enabled harness bundles (e.g., Claude Code, Codex); first-party vendor ecosystems (e.g., NVIDIA, Databricks); and widely-used open-source catalogs11 1 Marketplace/catalog bundles are assembled from public marketplaces [40] where users install multiple third-party skills together..

Across these monitored executions, Vigil surfaced 34 confirmed, real-world policy-violating runs out of 44 alerts. These violations include both skill-attributed defects, such as missing or conflicting bundle specifications, and agent-attributed failures, where the agent does not preserve or enforce a stated skill rule at runtime. We have a responsibility to disclose skill-attributed findings to affected maintainers through available channels. For agent-attributed failures, the skill specification already states the rule; the issue is that the agent runtime does not enforce it. One skill-attributed issue has been acknowledged by NVIDIA.

For each bundle, we used the BenchFlow SDK [41] to mount the skill documents in a Docker container and replaced external CLIs with logging stubs. In this replay-safe study, Vigil identifies the call it would block in a live deployment and outputs the offending witness before the stubbed effect is released. The 34 confirmed violations fall into three recurring patterns:

  1. 1.

    composition-level obligations missing across otherwise coherent skills;

  2. 2.

    persistent policy obligations lost across a task-driven trace;

  3. 3.

    stated skill rules not operationalized during execution.

Table IIIseparates failure origin: the first three findings expose specification gaps, where skill documents leave obligations underspecified or conflicting, while the last three expose agent execution gaps, where specifications state rules but agents fail to enforce them. We examine two in depth.

Case study 1: composition-level underspecification (Trail of Bits / NVIDIA). The first case concerns a 15-skill fuzzing bundle drawn from Trail of Bits’ open-source testing-handbook skills [27]. The bundle combines address-sanitizer, aflpp, and libfuzzer. The relevant skill documents state that AddressSanitizer maps, but does not reserve, 16+ TB of virtual address space [42], and instruct agents to disable the corresponding fuzzer memory limit when ASan is enabled: -m none for AFL++ and -rss_limit_mb=0 for libFuzzer. These requirements appear under different flag names and mechanisms (RLIMIT_AS for AFL++ and an RSS watchdog for libFuzzer), and the skill documents do not state the cross-skill obligation explicitly. In the probed trace, the agent compiled with -fsanitize=address but invoked both fuzzers without the required memory-limit-disabling flags. This configuration can silently invalidate the campaign. Under a global policy derived from the LLVM AddressSanitizer warning on memory-limiting tools [43], any fuzzer invocation after an ASan-instrumented compilation must explicitly disable the corresponding fuzzer memory limit. Vigil localizes the violation to the misconfigured fuzzer invocation. We reported a similar composition-level issue for NVIDIA’s skills, where a missing liveness specification caused repeated Slurm GPU submissions after evaluation failures; NVIDIA acknowledged this as a real cost concern.

Case study 2: missed prerequisite in execution (Databricks). The second case concerns a precondition violation in a Databricks skill bundle [26]. The databricks-core skill states an explicit precondition: “If the CLI is missing or outdated (< v0.292.0), stop immediately and do not attempt workarounds.” However, operational skills such as databricks-dabs and databricks-pipelines instruct the agent to run commands like databricks bundle deploy without referencing this version gate. In the probed trace, the agent’s version check returned a non-matching result, yet the agent proceeded to execute databricks commands. The applicable policy is a Precedence property: every databricks command must be preceded by a successful version check confirming CLI ≥\geq 0.292. The probed trace contains no such event, so Vigil catches the gap and blocks the deployment. The gate exists precisely because operational commands can misbehave on an outdated CLI; an agent that skips it can leave a bundle deployment half-applied.

VIII Related Work

Vigil builds on runtime enforcement for AI agents, authorization policy languages, and agent-skill security, but differs by grounding each policy in the observed trace.

Runtime enforcement for AI agents. Runtime enforcement moves AI-agent safety beyond prompt-level guidance to mechanisms that monitor tool use, constrain data influence, and enforce policies [44, 45]. Action-boundary systems such as AgentSpec [14], Progent [15], Conseca [16], and PCAS [17] guard proposed tool calls or compile contextual policies into instrumented checks. Context- and data-aware systems such as CaMeL [18], IFC-based agents [19, 46], AgentArmor [47], and AgentSentry [48] constrain actions using isolation, provenance, program analysis, or temporal causal diagnostics. Together, they decide whether proposed actions proceed, are sanitized, or are constrained by policy, provenance, isolation, or data flow.

Execution-level work [20, 49, 21] treats trajectories, effects, and world-state updates as the object of analysis. However, they use executions mainly as objects to classify or validate, rather than as contexts that shape enforcement. Vigil instead grounds each behavioral specification in the observed trace, refining the policy to the concrete run and capturing relational or temporal violations in executions.

Policy languages. Policy languages express security rules over users, actions, resources, and conditions while leaving enforcement to a separate monitor or decision procedure [50, 31, 51]. Cedar [52] provides a domain-specific language for fine-grained authorization policies, and major cloud platforms such as AWS IAM [53], Azure RBAC [54], and Google Cloud IAM [55] provide established policy languages for cloud resources. Zelkova [56] further shows that IAM-style policies can be given formal semantics and checked with SMT. However, these languages operate at the resource-authorization level: they decide whether a principal may perform an action on a resource under a set of attributes. Agent skill policies require a lower-level execution view: their policy object is a finite run with tool outputs, argument relations, and temporal ordering across calls, not a single authorization request.

Recent agent policy languages adapt policy ideas to agent actions: AgentSpec [14] and Progent [15] express action-level rules, while Conseca [16] and PCAS [17] generate or compile contextual policies for agent tasks. However, existing agent policy languages typically tie policies to a relatively fixed action or task context. Vigil instead treats the observed trace as the policy context, so the enforceable specification can be refined online as the run unfolds.

Agent skill security. Agent skills package procedural knowledge, instructions, executable code, and resources into reusable capabilities; this expands the agent security boundary from model responses and tool APIs to the skill package itself [57, 58]. Recent studies characterize skill architectures and lifecycle risks [57, 58, 59], and show that public skill ecosystems contain vulnerable, malicious, and harmful skills [60, 61, 62]. Recent systems audit or benchmark these risks: Skill-Inject [23] studies skill-file injection, AgentTrap [63] evaluates runtime trust failures, SkillProbe [64] audits marketplace skills, and Semia [65] converts skill text and structure into Datalog for static analysis. Closest to our setting, Sefz [9] shows that benign inputs can trigger specification violations when a skill breaks its own natural-language guardrails. Vigil complements this line by turning such behavioral requirements into runtime enforcement. Instead of searching for inputs that expose a violation, Vigil grounds the specification in the observed trace and checks whether the concrete run satisfies it.

IX Conclusion

We presented Vigil, a runtime reference monitor that makes agent-skill behavioral specifications executable. Vigil grounds each specification in the agent’s own execution trace and checks it with SMT, returning a localized witness when a run violates the policy. On real LLM-agent runs, Vigil detects trace-level violations that single-call defenses miss (95.8% recall at 89.6% precision) and surfaces 34 confirmed violations across deployed skill ecosystems, including one specification defect acknowledged by NVIDIA. Agent skills are still trusted to keep the contracts they declare; Vigil makes those contracts enforceable at runtime.

Appendix A Labeling Protocol for SB+SI

We construct SB+SI by combining violation-oriented candidate mining with randomly sampled benign executions. For SkillsBench, we first screen the released task-performance trajectories for cases in which the skill documentation states a behavioral obligation that can be checked against an execution trace, such as an ordering requirement, prerequisite check, argument constraint, or artifact-use rule. This screen is used to find candidate violations and excludes tasks whose specification only describes task success, user preference, or high-level quality criteria without an enforceable trace-level obligation. For Skill-Inject, which does not release raw trajectories, we replay its tasks in Claude Code and apply the same trace-level inclusion criteria to the recorded executions.

To construct the benign class, we randomly sample executions from the same benchmark sources and manually inspect them against the corresponding skill specifications. A randomly sampled execution is retained as benign only when the relevant behavioral obligation is satisfied, is not triggered, or no trace-checkable obligation applies. We discard sampled executions when the trace lacks the evidence needed to judge the obligation, when the specification is ambiguous, or when the apparent failure is only a task-quality error rather than a behavioral-policy violation.

All retained cases are manually labeled from the skill documentation, the execution trace, and any produced artifacts visible to the monitor. A trajectory is labeled violating only when the recorded execution contains a concrete event sequence that contradicts the skill’s stated behavioral specification. We use a conservative labeling rule: a case is retained as violating only when the violated obligation and responsible event sequence are both identifiable from the trace; otherwise, the case is excluded rather than adjudicated into either class. This process produces 152 labeled executions in SB+SI: 72 policy-violating trajectories and 80 benign trajectories.

Appendix B Baseline Adaptation Protocol

We keep the policy source and execution trace fixed across all systems, and score every verdict against the same ground-truth label. For each SB+SI case, AgentSpec and Progent receive the closest faithful rule encoding supported by their action-boundary interfaces. Policies over the pending action, its arguments, or local trigger conditions are encoded directly. Policies that require long-range artifact identity, historical data flow, or evidence outside the pending action are encoded as the strongest action-boundary approximation, without adding Vigil-style trace memory to the baseline.

The LLM-as-judge baseline receives only the inputs available before enforcement: the full execution trace, the skill specification, and the same policy-relevant context available to Vigil. It returns a binary violation verdict with a short rationale, but does not receive Vigil’s alert, compiled policy, SMT witness, or the ground-truth label.

Appendix C Specification-Compilation Prompt Template

Vigil uses the language model only to draft candidate policy documents, not to judge whether a trace violates a policy. Figure 9 shows an abridged template of the prompt interface.

Every drafted PolicyDocument is parsed and validated against the observed signature before SMT encoding; invalid, ill-typed, or unsupported clauses are rejected by deterministic components.
